reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods
chapter_title: Selection and Use of Drilled Shaft Foundations for Transportation Structures

sections.title: Purpose and Organization of Manual
sections.body: This technical manual provides a resource for engineers responsible for selection and design of drilled shaft foundations for transportation structures and serves as a reference for NHI training course No. 132014. It is an updated edition of FHWA-NHI-10-016 (Brown et al., 2010). Major updates include: consistency with 2017a AASHTO standards; revised Chapter 2 (site investigation focused on drilled shaft-specific requirements); updated construction chapters 3-6; updated concrete chapter 7 with advances in SCC technology; new Chapter 8 (design roadmap); updated lateral design in Chapter 9 with seismic content; updated axial design equations in Chapter 10; updated group design in Chapter 11; Chapter 12 structural design now includes STM for rock sockets per 2017 AASHTO; expanded load testing guidance in Chapter 13; updated specifications in Chapter 14; updated inspection in Chapter 15; Chapter 16 includes thermal integrity profiling (TIP); Chapter 17 covers assessment and remediation with case histories; Chapter 18 updates cost estimation. The manual is organized into: Overview (Ch 1), Site Characterization (Ch 2), Construction (Ch 3-7), Design (Ch 8-12), and Quality Assurance (Ch 13-18). A comprehensive design example is presented in Appendix A.
key_points: Updated to be consistent with 2017a AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications
All design presented in LRFD format
Replaces FHWA-NHI-10-016 (2010 edition)
18 chapters covering construction, design, and quality assurance
Comprehensive design example in Appendix A

sections.title: Deep Foundation Alternatives
sections.body: Drilled shafts are cast-in-place deep foundation elements constructed in a drilled hole stabilized to allow placement of reinforcing and concrete. Alternatives include: (1) Driven piles — prefabricated elements (steel H, pipe, prestressed concrete) 12-60 in diameter, displace soil, cannot penetrate hard material or rock, no hole stability concern; guidelines in FHWA NHI-16-009 (Hannigan et al., 2016). (2) Micropiles — drilled piles <12 in diameter using high-strength steel rod or pipe grouted into bearing formation; can drill into hard rock; guidelines in FHWA-NHI-05-039 (Sabatini et al., 2005). (3) Continuous flight auger (CFA) and drilled displacement piles — 12-30 in diameter, formed by screwing auger/tool into ground and grouting through hollow center; no open hole during construction; guidelines in FHWA GEC-8 (Brown et al., 2007). Drilled shafts are distinguished by substantially larger size, frequent use as single shaft without a pile cap, and installation into hard bearing strata.
key_points: Driven piles: 12-60 in diameter, displace soil, cannot penetrate hard materials
Micropiles: <12 in diameter, high-strength steel rod grouted into bearing formation
CFA/drilled displacement piles: 12-30 in diameter, no open hole during construction
Drilled shafts: larger size, single shaft without cap, hard bearing strata

sections.title: Drilled Shaft Foundations — Description and History
sections.body: Drilled shaft foundations are formed by excavating a hole typically 3 to 12 ft in diameter, inspecting soil or rock, and constructing a cast-in-place reinforced concrete foundation. They support axial forces through side shear and end bearing resistance and provide substantial resistance to lateral and overturning forces. Commonly used to depths of 200 ft, can extend to 300 ft or more. Also called drilled piers, caissons, cast-in-drilled-hole piles (CIDH — Caltrans), and bored piles (Europe). Historical development: caisson construction used for centuries; pneumatic caissons pioneered in the US by James Eads in St. Louis (1869) and Roebling on Brooklyn Bridge (1870s). First building on 'caissons' was Kansas City City Hall (1890) — 92 caissons, 4-ft diameter to limestone at ~50 ft. Chicago 'caisson' method developed 1893 by William Sooy Smith. Gow Construction Co. (founded 1899) pioneered telescoping casing. Machine-drilled shafts more widespread from 1930s; bucket-auger machines common in California. A.H. Beck Company began using drilled shafts in 1932. Modern construction now employs underwater concrete placement, eliminating need for dry excavation or worker entry.
key_points: Typical diameter: 3-12 ft; typical depth: up to 200 ft (300 ft possible)
Also known as drilled piers, caissons, CIDH piles (Caltrans), bored piles (Europe)
First US application: Kansas City City Hall (1890), 4-ft diameter shafts to limestone
Machine drilling widespread from 1930s
Modern construction uses underwater concrete, no dry excavation required

sections.title: Selection of Drilled Shafts
sections.body: Drilled shafts are most efficiently utilized where a strong bearing layer is present. Single shaft support avoids need for a pile cap with excavation and excavation support. Foundations over water can often be constructed through permanent casing avoiding a cofferdam. Can be installed into hard, scour-resistant formations below scourable soil.

sections.title: Applications
sections.body: Bridge Foundations: favorable conditions include cohesive soils with deep groundwater; stratigraphy with firm bearing stratum within 100 ft; widening/congested spaces where small footprint is needed (single shaft avoids large pile cap footprint and costly excavation support); foundations over water through permanent casing; very high axial or lateral loads; deep scour conditions where driven piles are impractical; restricted access or low headroom. Other Applications: sound walls, signs, high mast lighting where overturning dominates — drilled shafts do not require great length; retaining structures — wall footing on single row of shafts without cap, or soldier beams with precast panels; secant pile walls — every second shaft unreinforced, remaining shafts cut overlap into first set and are reinforced; tangent pile walls without overlap for non-watertight applications; landslide stabilization — drilled shaft wall or rows of shafts across slip surface to provide restraining force.
key_points: Bridge foundations: favorable in cohesive soils, firm bearing within 100 ft, deep scour, high loads
Single shaft eliminates pile cap — smaller footprint, no cap excavation
Retaining walls: single row without cap, or soldier beams with precast panels
Secant piles: alternating reinforced/unreinforced shafts with overlap for watertight wall
Landslide stabilization: shaft wall across slip surface

sections.title: Advantages and Limitations
sections.body: Drilled shafts allow direct inspection of bearing material to confirm nature of bearing stratum. Most significant limitations relate to sensitivity of construction to ground conditions and importance of maintaining standard of care during installation.
key_points: Advantages: easy construction in cohesive materials and most rock; wide range of ground conditions; visual inspection of bearing stratum; extremely high axial resistance possible; excellent flexural strength; small footprint without pile cap; low noise and vibration (urban applications); penetrates below scour zone; easily adjusted for variable conditions

Limitations: construction sensitive to groundwater or difficult drilling conditions; performance influenced by construction method; no direct measurement of axial resistance during installation; high-resistance load testing is challenging and expensive; structural integrity requires careful construction and QA/QC; single shaft lacks redundancy requiring high reliability; requires experienced specialty contractor; may not be efficient in deep soft soils without bearing formation; requires thorough site investigation

sections.title: Keys to Successful Use of Drilled Shafts
sections.body: Five keys to successful construction and design of drilled shafts: (1) Subsurface Investigation — thorough investigation required for design and for selection of appropriate construction tools and methods; must address groundwater level, soil permeability, rock hardness, obstructions, and geologic features; rock characterization is challenging since shafts often bear in hard soils or rock (Chapter 2). (2) Knowledge of Construction Techniques — engineers and project managers must thoroughly understand construction methods for constructible, cost-effective, and reliable designs (Chapters 3-7). (3) Design for Constructability and Reliability — a robust design is simple to execute and accommodates variations in subsurface conditions; load testing confirms design methodology and reduces risk (Chapter 13); constructible designs are more cost-effective (Chapter 18). (4) Appropriate Specifications — must be constructible, provide means for quality assurance, and achieve required performance; must incorporate understanding of construction techniques and their potential influence (Chapter 14, Appendix D). (5) Quality Assurance — rigorous program of inspection and testing is essential; inspection and tests described in Chapters 15-16; assessment and acceptance in Chapter 17 with remediation techniques.
key_points: 1. Thorough subsurface investigation — design AND constructability
2. Knowledge of construction techniques — essential for constructible design
3. Design for constructability and reliability — load testing confirms design
4. Appropriate specifications — constructible, achievable, with QA provisions
5. Quality assurance — inspection, testing, assessment, remediation
sections.applicability: Project planning and design process; applies to all drilled shaft projects

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter 1 introduced drilled shaft foundations with brief history of US development. Applications for transportation structures presented with advantages and limitations vs. other deep foundations. Keys to successful use emphasize design for constructability. Design is presented in LRFD format consistent with 2017 AASHTO standards.
key_points: LRFD design framework consistent with 2017 AASHTO
Design for constructability is the recurring theme throughout the manual
